claim: Output signals of neural circuits, including the retina, are shaped by a combination of excitatory and inhibitory signals.
source: Output signals of neural circuits, including the retina, are shaped by a combination of excitatory and inhibitory signals.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural circuit function that draws from established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Inhibitory signals can act presynaptically on axon terminals to control neurotransmitter release and regulate circuit function.
source: Inhibitory signals can act presynaptically on axon terminals to control neurotransmitter release and regulate circuit function.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about presynaptic inhibition mechanisms.

claim: Selective loss of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition causes an enhanced sensitivity of light-evoked responses from ON alpha ganglion cells.
source: Selective loss of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition causes an enhanced sensitivity and slower kinetics of light-evoked responses from ON alpha ganglion cells thus highlighting the role of presynaptic inhibition in gain control and temporal filtering of sensory signals in a key neural circuit in the mammalian retina.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Selective loss of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition causes slower kinetics of light-evoked responses from ON alpha ganglion cells.
source: Selective loss of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition causes an enhanced sensitivity and slower kinetics of light-evoked responses from ON alpha ganglion cells thus highlighting the role of presynaptic inhibition in gain control and temporal filtering of sensory signals in a key neural circuit in the mammalian retina.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Presynaptic inhibition is a common motif by which inhibition acts in neural circuits at the axon terminals of presynaptic neurons where it regulates synaptic release and controls the input-output relationship of a neural circuit.
source: A common motif by which inhibition acts in neural circuits is at the axon terminals of presynaptic neurons where it regulates synaptic release and controls the input-output relationship of a neural circuit (Fink et al., 2014; MacDermott et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Presynaptic inhibition is widely used in the retina and is mediated by inhibitory retinal interneurons called amacrine cells.
source: This motif of inhibition called presynaptic inhibition is widely used in the retina and is mediated by inhibitory retinal interneurons called amacrine cells (ACs) (Diamond and Lukasiewicz, 2012; Eggers and Lukasiewicz, 2011; Eggers et al., 2007; Jadzinsky and Baccus, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Amacrine cells make synaptic contacts on the axon terminals of glutamatergic second-order neurons called bipolar cells.
source: ACs make synaptic contacts on the axon terminals of glutamatergic second-order neurons called bipolar cells (BCs) which relay rod and cone photoreceptor signals to retinal output neurons called retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) (Demb and Singer, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Bipolar cells relay rod and cone photoreceptor signals to retinal output neurons called retinal ganglion cells.
source: ACs make synaptic contacts on the axon terminals of glutamatergic second-order neurons called bipolar cells (BCs) which relay rod and cone photoreceptor signals to retinal output neurons called retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) (Demb and Singer, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ON bipolar cells depolarize in response to a light increment.
source: Axon terminals of 'ON' BCs – that depolarize in response to a light increment – and 'OFF' BCs – that hyperpolarize in response to a light increment – each stratify at different retinal laminae (Demb and Singer, 2015; Hoon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: OFF bipolar cells hyperpolarize in response to a light increment.
source: Axon terminals of 'ON' BCs – that depolarize in response to a light increment – and 'OFF' BCs – that hyperpolarize in response to a light increment – each stratify at different retinal laminae (Demb and Singer, 2015; Hoon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ON and OFF bipolar cell axon terminals each stratify at different retinal laminae.
source: Axon terminals of 'ON' BCs – that depolarize in response to a light increment – and 'OFF' BCs – that hyperpolarize in response to a light increment – each stratify at different retinal laminae (Demb and Singer, 2015; Hoon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Different bipolar cell types are used to route dim light (rod bipolar; ON type) and day light (cone bipolar; ON and OFF types) visual signals.
source: Of note, different BC types are also used to route dim light (rod bipolar; ON type) and day light (cone bipolar; ON and OFF types) visual signals (Euler et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ON sustained alpha ganglion cells depolarize and respond with an increase in action potential firing to light increments.
source: ONα GCs depolarize and respond with an increase in action potential firing to light increments (Grimes et al., 2014b; Murphy and Rieke, 2006; van Wyk et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The ONα GC pathway is the most sensitive dim light retinal pathway.
source: This ONα GC pathway is not only the most sensitive dim light retinal pathway (Smeds et al., 2019): rod photoreceptors -> rod bipolar cells (RBCs) -> AII amacrine -> ON cone bipolar cell (CBC) -> ONα GC; but also one that routes visual signals directly from cone photoreceptors via ON CBCs for mediating day light vision (Demb and Singer, 2015; Grimes et al., 2014b; Schmidt et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The ONα GC pathway routes visual signals directly from cone photoreceptors via ON CBCs for mediating day light vision.
source: This ONα GC pathway is not only the most sensitive dim light retinal pathway (Smeds et al., 2019): rod photoreceptors -> rod bipolar cells (RBCs) -> AII amacrine -> ON cone bipolar cell (CBC) -> ONα GC; but also one that routes visual signals directly from cone photoreceptors via ON CBCs for mediating day light vision (Demb and Singer, 2015; Grimes et al., 2014b; Schmidt et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RBCs and ON CBCs predominantly express GABAA and GABAC receptors at their axon terminals.
source: RBCs and ON CBCs predominantly express GABAA and GABAC receptors at their axon terminals, whereas OFF CBCs predominantly express GABAA and glycine receptors (GlyR) at their axon terminals (Eggers and Lukasiewicz, 2006; Fletcher et al., 1998; Hoon et al., 2015; Lukasiewicz et al., 2004; Wässle et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: OFF CBCs predominantly express GABAA and glycine receptors at their axon terminals.
source: RBCs and ON CBCs predominantly express GABAA and GABAC receptors at their axon terminals, whereas OFF CBCs predominantly express GABAA and glycine receptors (GlyR) at their axon terminals (Eggers and Lukasiewicz, 2006; Fletcher et al., 1998; Hoon et al., 2015; Lukasiewicz et al., 2004; Wässle et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A17 amacrine cells make GABAergic feedback synapses on RBC axon terminals.
source: In the primary rod (dim-light) pathway, presynaptic inhibition has been particularly well characterized where a specialized AC type, the A17 AC, makes GABAergic feedback synapses on RBC axon terminals (Grimes et al., 2014a; Grimes et al., 2010; Grimes et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A17-mediated feedback inhibition has been proposed to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of the feedforward excitatory output from RBC to AII amacrine cell near visual threshold.
source: This A17-mediated feedback inhibition has been proposed to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of the feedforward excitatory output from RBC to AII amacrine cell near visual threshold, extend the luminance range over which RBC-AII synapses compute contrast gain, and mediate center-surround inhibition (Grimes et al., 2015; Oesch and Diamond, 2019; Völgyi et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A17-mediated feedback inhibition extends the luminance range over which RBC-AII synapses compute contrast gain.
source: This A17-mediated feedback inhibition has been proposed to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of the feedforward excitatory output from RBC to AII amacrine cell near visual threshold, extend the luminance range over which RBC-AII synapses compute contrast gain, and mediate center-surround inhibition (Grimes et al., 2015; Oesch and Diamond, 2019; Völgyi et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A17-mediated feedback inhibition mediates center-surround inhibition.
source: This A17-mediated feedback inhibition has been proposed to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of the feedforward excitatory output from RBC to AII amacrine cell near visual threshold, extend the luminance range over which RBC-AII synapses compute contrast gain, and mediate center-surround inhibition (Grimes et al., 2015; Oesch and Diamond, 2019; Völgyi et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Perturbing GABAC receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition alters the dynamic range of the light-evoked responses of RGCs for both rod and cone-mediated signaling.
source: In addition, a few studies have shown that perturbing GABAC receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition alters the dynamic range of the light-evoked responses of RGCs for both rod and cone-mediated signaling (Oesch and Diamond, 2019; Pan et al., 2016; Sagdullaev et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GABAA receptors expressed in the axon terminals of ON BCs contain α1 and γ2 subunits.
source: GABAA receptors expressed in the axon terminals of ON BCs contain α1 and γ2 subunits (Hoon et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the KO mice, GABAAα1 expression is selectively reduced from the ON sub-lamina of the inner plexiform layer.
source: Immunolabeling with GABAAα1 receptor subunit specific antibody clearly showed the selective reduction in GABAAα1 expression from the ON sub-lamina of the inner plexiform layer (IPL) in the KO mice (Figure 1B), whereas the GABAAα1 expression in the OFF sub-lamina remained unperturbed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GABAAα1 expression in the OFF sub-lamina remained unperturbed in the KO mice.
source: Immunolabeling with GABAAα1 receptor subunit specific antibody clearly showed the selective reduction in GABAAα1 expression from the ON sub-lamina of the inner plexiform layer (IPL) in the KO mice (Figure 1B), whereas the GABAAα1 expression in the OFF sub-lamina remained unperturbed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is near-complete absence of GABAAα1 receptor subunit expression from RBC boutons in the KO retina.
source: Co-labeling of GABAAα1 with the RBC marker, protein kinase C (PKC), revealed near-complete absence of GABAAα1 receptor subunit expression from RBC boutons in the KO retina (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GABAC receptor expression was unchanged in KO RBC terminals.
source: Despite the loss of GABAA receptors in KO RBC terminals, GABAC receptor expression was unchanged in KO RBC terminals (Figure 1D; quantifications of percentage GABAC volume occupancy).
evidence: This is supported by immunolabeling and quantification data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Puffing GABA on the axon terminals of RBCs elicited smaller currents in the KO retina.
source: Puffing GABA on the axon terminals of RBCs elicited smaller currents in the KO retina.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: The decrease in total GABA-evoked current in KO RBCs is due to a drastic reduction of the GABAA receptor-mediated current with unaltered GABAC currents.
source: Upon application of a selective GABAC receptor blocker, TPMPA, we found that this decrease in total GABA-evoked current is due to a drastic reduction of the GABAA receptor-mediated current with unaltered GABAC currents in KO RBC terminals (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Light evoked excitatory currents from OFF alpha transient GCs showed no differences in amplitude between KO and wildtype retina.
source: To confirm that GABAA receptors remain unaltered in the OFF sublamina, we performed whole-cell voltage clamp recordings of light evoked excitatory currents from OFF alpha transient GCs (a measure of the OFF BC output) which showed no differences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) in amplitude between KO and wildtype adult littermate control (WT) retina.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of GABAA receptors is not impacted across AC and GC processes in the KO retina.
source: Upon quantification of the percentage occupancy of GABAAβ2/3 receptors across ON-laminating AC and GC processes we observed comparable receptor amounts across genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) confirming that expression of GABAA receptors is not impacted across AC and GC processes in the KO retina.
evidence: This is supported by immunolabeling and quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: In the KO retina, the majority of the GABAA receptors lost from the IPL are from RBC and T6 CBC terminals.
source: This means that in the KO retina, the majority of the GABAA receptors lost from the IPL are from RBC and T6 CBC terminals (Figure 1; and see Hoon et al., 2015), thus providing a unique opportunity to study how GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition alters the function of a specific retinal circuit, i.e. the ONα GC circuit (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The characteristic response of an ONα GC to a light step has two distinct kinetic components – a fast transient phase and steady-state sustained phase.
source: The characteristic response of an ONα GC to a light step (0.5 s duration) has two distinct kinetic components – a fast transient phase and steady-state sustained phase – which results in action potential firing throughout the duration of the light stimulus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The biphasic response to a sustained dim light step has previously been observed in the excitatory currents of the AII amacrine cell and reflects the intrinsic synaptic properties of the RBC to AII amacrine cell ribbon synapse.
source: Such a biphasic response to a sustained dim light step has previously been observed in the excitatory currents of the AII amacrine cell and reflects the intrinsic synaptic properties of the RBC to AII amacrine cell ribbon synapse (Oesch and Diamond, 2011, Oesch and Diamond, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The transient component of the ONα GC response has been attributed to encode contrast.
source: Furthermore, the transient component has been attributed to encode contrast whereas the sustained component has been shown to encode the absolute luminance (Oesch and Diamond, 2011Oesch and Diamond, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The sustained component of the ONα GC response has been shown to encode the absolute luminance.
source: Furthermore, the transient component has been attributed to encode contrast whereas the sustained component has been shown to encode the absolute luminance (Oesch and Diamond, 2011Oesch and Diamond, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the KO retina, there is a sizeable increase in the spike response of ONα GCs for both its transient and sustained component.
source: In the KO retina, there is a sizeable increase in the spike response of ONα GCs for both its transient and sustained component (Figure 2C and D; see 'Materials and methods' for details).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: There was no significant difference in the kinetics of the ONα GC spike responses between KO and WT retina under dim light conditions.
source: There was no significant difference in the kinetics of the ONα GC spike responses between KO and WT retina under dim light conditions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The heightened response to the dim light stimuli is more prominent in the excitatory synaptic currents of ONα GCs in the KO retina with nearly a twofold increase in the amplitude of the response in the KO retinas compared to that in the WT retinas.
source: The heightened response to the dim light stimuli is in fact more prominent in the excitatory synaptic currents of ONα GCs in the KO retina with nearly a twofold increase in the amplitude of the response in the KO retinas compared to that in the WT retinas (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Both the sustained and transient response components for the ONα GC are equally affected in the KO retina.
source: Both the sustained and transient response components for the ONα GC are equally affected in the KO retina and hence the ratio of sustained to transient response remained unchanged between the WT and the KO retina for light evoked excitatory synaptic currents as well as for spike output (Figure 2D and H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2D and H.

claim: The ratio of sustained to transient response remained unchanged between the WT and the KO retina for light evoked excitatory synaptic currents as well as for spike output.
source: Both the sustained and transient response components for the ONα GC are equally affected in the KO retina and hence the ratio of sustained to transient response remained unchanged between the WT and the KO retina for light evoked excitatory synaptic currents as well as for spike output (Figure 2D and H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2D and H.

claim: The time to peak of the ONα GC dim light evoked excitatory synaptic currents remained unchanged between the WT and the KO retina.
source: We next estimated the kinetics of the ONα GC dim light evoked excitatory synaptic currents and found that the time to peak of the current response remained unchanged between the WT and the KO retina similar to that for the spike output (Figure 2I; see Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Both the ONα GC spike output and the excitatory synaptic currents in the KO retina showed a marked increase over a considerable range of dim light flash intensities.
source: Both the ONα GC spike output and the excitatory synaptic currents in the KO retina showed a marked increase over a considerable range of dim light flash intensities (Figure 2K and M).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2K and M.

claim: Light-triggered output from the RBC terminals is increased in absence of GABAA receptors across a wide range of dim light levels albeit not for the dimmest flashes.
source: This indicates that light-triggered output from the RBC terminals is increased in absence of GABAA receptors across a wide range of dim light levels albeit not for the dimmest flashes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 2K and M.

claim: Enhancement of both the transient and sustained component of the ONα GC response to a sustained dim light stimulus indicates that perhaps both contrast and luminance encoding are altered at the dim light levels.
source: Moreover, enhancement of both the transient and sustained component of the ONα GC response to a sustained dim light stimulus indicates that perhaps both contrast and luminance encoding are altered at the dim light levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and previous literature about the functional roles of transient and sustained components.

claim: Response kinetics remain unaltered in absence of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition at dim light levels.
source: Although the amplitude of the dim light evoked responses is perturbed, response kinetics remain unaltered in absence of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2E and I.

claim: GABAA receptors at the RBC terminal play a key role in regulating the strength of dim light signals received by the ONα GCs presumably by controlling synaptic release from the RBC terminal.
source: These results show that GABAA receptors at the RBC terminal play a key role in regulating the strength of dim light signals received by the ONα GCs presumably by controlling synaptic release from the RBC terminal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and knowledge of presynaptic inhibition mechanisms.

claim: A nearly twofold increase in the peak firing rate of the ONα GC in the KO retina compared to that in the WT retina was observed at cone-dominated light levels.
source: We observed a nearly twofold increase in the peak firing rate of the ONα GC in the KO retina compared to that in the WT retina.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No systematic difference in the sustained phase of the spike response of ONα GCs between WT and KO retina was observed at cone-dominated light levels.
source: However, we did not see a systematic difference in the sustained phase of the spike response of ONα GCs between WT and KO retina (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The time to peak of the ONα GC spike responses in the KO retina were significantly slower than in the WT retina at cone-dominated light levels.
source: Interestingly, the time to peak of the ONα GC spike responses in the KO retina were significantly slower than in the WT retina in contrast to our earlier observations under dim light conditions (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both the transient and sustained phase of the light-evoked excitatory synaptic current were ~2-fold larger in the KO retina compared to that in the WT retina at cone-dominated light levels.
source: Both the transient and sustained phase of the light-evoked excitatory synaptic current were ~2-fold larger in the KO retina compared to that in the WT retina (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The ratio of the sustained-to-transient phase of the ONα GC response remained unchanged between KO and WT retina at cone-dominated light levels.
source: The ratio of the sustained-to-transient phase of the ONα GC response remained unchanged between KO and WT retina (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The time to peak of ONα GC excitatory currents was higher in the KO retina than in the WT retina at cone-dominated light levels.
source: Upon comparing the response kinetics of ONα GC excitatory currents between KO and WT retina, we observed that the time to peak was higher in the KO retina than in the WT retina similar to the effects on the spike output seen earlier (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The time of onset of the sustained phase of the light-evoked excitatory currents in ONα GC did not show any significant changes between KO and WT retina.
source: We further quantified the time of onset of the sustained phase of the light-evoked excitatory currents in ONα GC but did not observe any significant changes between KO and WT retina (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The decay time of the flash-evoked ONα GC excitatory synaptic currents was significantly longer in KO compared to WT retina.
source: In addition to the longer time taken to reach peak response (Figure 3K), we also found that the decay time of the flash-evoked ONα GC excitatory synaptic currents (from the peak to the baseline) was significantly longer in KO compared to WT retina (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition regulates both the activation and recovery of the cone-mediated signals at the BC to ONα GC synapse.
source: This suggests that GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition regulates both the activation and recovery of the cone-mediated signals at the BC to ONα GC synapse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing changes in time to peak and decay time.

claim: The amplitude of the response overshoot from the baseline showed no difference between ONα GCs in KO and WT retina.
source: We estimated the amplitude of the response overshoot from the baseline and observed no difference between ONα GCs in KO and WT retina (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: There was no change in light-evoked postsynaptic inhibition in ONα GC in the KO retina compared to that in the WT retina.
source: There was no change in light-evoked postsynaptic inhibition in ONα GC in the KO retina compared to that in the WT retina indicating that increase in the excitatory inputs most likely cause the increase in the spike output of ONα GC light responses in the KO retina (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Increase in the excitatory inputs most likely cause the increase in the spike output of ONα GC light responses in the KO retina.
source: There was no change in light-evoked postsynaptic inhibition in ONα GC in the KO retina compared to that in the WT retina indicating that increase in the excitatory inputs most likely cause the increase in the spike output of ONα GC light responses in the KO retina (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing unchanged inhibition but increased excitation.

claim: Loss of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition alters the amplitude of both rod- and cone-driven signals but only the time course of cone-driven signals received by the ONα GCs.
source: These results suggest that loss of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition alters the amplitude of both rod- and cone-driven signals but only the time course of cone-driven signals received by the ONα GCs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The time course of the ONα GC excitatory current response in the KO retina is considerably slower than in the WT retina at cone light levels.
source: At cone light levels, linear filters show that the time course of the ONα GC excitatory current response in the KO retina is considerably slower than in the WT retina (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by linear-nonlinear model analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both the time to peak and the decay time of the linear filters were significantly longer for ONα GC in KO retina compared to WT retina at cone light levels.
source: Both the time to peak and the decay time of the linear filters were significantly longer for ONα GC in KO retina compared to WT retina (Figure 4C) similar to the above results from the responses to brief light flashes (Figure 3K,L).
evidence: This is supported by linear-nonlinear model analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Lack of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition alters the temporal filtering of the T6 CBC output and hence the excitatory inputs in the ONα GCs by likely attenuating higher frequencies more and lower frequencies less.
source: This suggests that lack of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition alters the temporal filtering of the T6 CBC output and hence the excitatory inputs in the ONα GCs by likely attenuating higher frequencies more and lower frequencies less.
evidence: This is an inference based on the linear filter analysis.

claim: The response range (dynamic range) of the excitatory currents for the given range of contrasts was ~2-fold larger for the ONα GCs in the KO retina in comparison to their counterparts in the WT retina at cone light levels.
source: This response range, i.e. dynamic range of the excitatory currents for the given range of contrasts, was ~2-fold larger for the ONα GCs in the KO retina in comparison to their counterparts in the WT retina (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by linear-nonlinear model analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The nonlinearities of the ONα GC response in KO retina had a steeper slope and the slope differed by a factor of ~2 compared to the ONα GC nonlinearities in WT retina at cone light levels.
source: The nonlinearities of the ONα GC response in KO retina had a steeper slope and upon quantification the slope differed by a factor of ~2 compared to the ONα GC nonlinearities in WT retina (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by linear-nonlinear model analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: GABAA presynaptic inhibition tightly regulates contrast sensitivity of the ONα GC excitatory inputs and restricts the response size used for encoding over a range of contrast.
source: These results suggest that GABAA presynaptic inhibition tightly regulates contrast sensitivity of the ONα GC excitatory inputs and restricts the response size used for encoding over a range of contrast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the linear-nonlinear model analysis.

claim: The nonlinearity of the ONα GC in the KO retina had a bigger response range than in WT retina under dim light background.
source: The nonlinearity of the ONα GC in the KO retina also had a bigger response range than in WT retina similar to that observed under cone-driven light levels (Figure 4K,L).
evidence: This is supported by linear-nonlinear model analysis shown in Figure 4K,L.

claim: The slope of the nonlinearity (contrast gain) was ~2-fold higher for the ONα GC in the KO retina than that in the WT retina under dim light background.
source: The slope of the nonlinearity, i.e. contrast gain was also ~2-fold higher for the ONα GC in the KO retina than that in the WT retina (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is supported by linear-nonlinear model analysis shown in Figure 4M.

claim: No significant difference in the kinetics of the linear filters between the genotypes was observed under dim light background.
source: However, no significant difference in the kinetics of the linear filters between the genotypes was observed (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by linear-nonlinear model analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Loss of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition at the RBC and T6 CBC terminal alters the contrast sensitivity and kinetics of the ONα GC excitatory inputs.
source: Thus, loss of GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition at the RBC and T6 CBC terminal alters the contrast sensitivity and kinetics of the ONα GC excitatory inputs.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data from Figure 4.

claim: The changes in response amplitude and kinetics observed at the level of ONα GC excitatory inputs in the KO retina are reflected in the spike output.
source: Importantly the changes in response amplitude and kinetics observed at the level of ONα GC excitatory inputs in the KO retina are reflected in the spike output which highlights the importance of GABAA presynaptic inhibition as a mechanism in shaping visual signals being transmitted out of the retina.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing excitatory current and spike output data.

claim: GABAA presynaptic inhibition is a key mechanism in shaping visual signals being transmitted out of the retina.
source: Importantly the changes in response amplitude and kinetics observed at the level of ONα GC excitatory inputs in the KO retina are reflected in the spike output which highlights the importance of GABAA presynaptic inhibition as a mechanism in shaping visual signals being transmitted out of the retina.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition is crucial for regulating the amplitude and contrast sensitivity of both rod and cone-driven signals routed to the ONα GCs.
source: We show that GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition is crucial for regulating the amplitude and contrast sensitivity of both rod and cone-driven signals routed to the ONα GCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: GABAA presynaptic inhibition shapes the kinetics of only cone-driven signals but not rod-driven signals reaching the ONα GCs.
source: Interestingly, GABAA presynaptic inhibition shapes the kinetics of only cone-driven signals but not rod-driven signals reaching the ONα GCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: GABAA presynaptic inhibition is a key mechanism of gain control and temporal filtering for the ONα GC retinal circuit.
source: Thus, GABAA presynaptic inhibition is a key mechanism of gain control and temporal filtering for the ONα GC retinal circuit.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: GABAA and GABAC receptors in ON BC terminals contribute to nearly equal amplitudes of GABA-evoked currents.
source: Several studies including our current study have shown that GABAA and GABAC receptors in ON BC terminals contribute to nearly equal amplitudes of GABA-evoked currents (Hoon et al., 2015; Sinha et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data from the current study.

claim: GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition plays an equally important role in regulating the dynamic range and contrast sensitivity as GABAC receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition for both the RBC output under dim light conditions as well as for cone-mediated signals via the ON CBC synapse.
source: In the current study, we show that GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition plays an equally important role in regulating the dynamic range and contrast sensitivity as GABAC receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition for both the RBC output under dim light conditions as well as for cone-mediated signals via the ON CBC synapse.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from the current study.

claim: GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition restricts the response range and contrast gain of ONα GC responses which could allow the ONα GC retinal circuit to encode over a wider range of contrast and luminance without being saturated.
source: GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition restricts the response range and contrast gain of ONα GC responses which could allow the ONα GC retinal circuit to encode over a wider range of contrast and luminance without being saturated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and knowledge of neural coding principles.

claim: Both GABAA and GABAC presynaptic inhibition play a key role in regulating response amplitude and contrast encoding under rod- and cone-dominant lighting conditions.
source: Thus, our results together with previous findings (Oesch and Diamond, 2019; Sagdullaev et al., 2006) suggest that both GABAA and GABAC presynaptic inhibition play a key role in regulating response amplitude and contrast encoding under rod- and cone-dominant lighting conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from the current study and previous literature.

claim: Signals originating in rod vs. cone photoreceptors exhibit remarkably distinct temporal characteristics with rod signals being substantially slower compared to cone signals.
source: Signals originating in rod vs. cone photoreceptors are known to exhibit remarkably distinct temporal characteristics with rod signals being substantially slower compared to cone signals (Cangiano et al., 2012; Ingram et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The time course of rod signals was nearly 2-fold slower than the cone-mediated signals in WT retina measured at the level of ONα GCs.
source: This difference is reflected in our results from both fixed intensity and randomly modulating stimuli where the time course of rod signals was nearly 2-fold slower than the cone-mediated signals in WT retina measured at the level of ONα GCs (Figure 2E and I vs. Figure 3D,H and K; Figure 4C vs J).
evidence: This is supported by data from Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: GABAA presynaptic inhibition speeds up the time course of cone-mediated signals but not rod-driven signals in the ONα GC retinal circuit.
source: Our findings show that GABAA presynaptic inhibition speeds up the time course of cone-mediated signals but not rod-driven signals in the ONα GC retinal circuit.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by data from Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Under dim light conditions where photons are sparse, a longer integration time of the rod signals by the downstream circuit may benefit signal detection.
source: This could be because under dim light conditions where photons are sparse, a longer integration time of the rod signals by the downstream circuit may benefit signal detection (Field et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Temporal filtering by mechanisms such as presynaptic inhibition could be detrimental to the detection of sparse signals such as single photons.
source: In this case, temporal filtering by mechanisms such as presynaptic inhibition could be detrimental to the detection of sparse signals such as single photons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the logic of signal detection.

claim: ONα GCs are one of the most sensitive GC types in the mouse retina under dim light conditions and comprise the major conduit for relaying single photon signals out of the retina.
source: In fact, recent studies have shown that ONα GCs are one of the most sensitive GC types in the mouse retina under dim light conditions and comprise the major conduit for relaying single photon signals out of the retina (Smeds et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Minimizing temporal filtering by GABAA presynaptic inhibition may help prolong the duration of signal integration and may improve sensitivity of the ONα GCs for single photon signaling in near complete darkness.
source: Hence, minimizing temporal filtering by GABAA presynaptic inhibition may help prolong the duration of signal integration and may improve sensitivity of the ONα GCs for single photon signaling in near complete darkness.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and knowledge of signal detection.

claim: GABAA presynaptic inhibition limits the response size and contrast gain while speeding up cone-driven signals reaching the ONα GCs.
source: Our results show that GABAA presynaptic inhibition limits the response size and contrast gain while speeding up cone-driven signals reaching the ONα GCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by data from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Encoding contrast with a smaller response amplitude might allow to effectively signal over a broader dynamic range of contrasts without being saturated.
source: First, encoding contrast with a smaller response amplitude might allow to effectively signal over a broader dynamic range of contrasts without being saturated.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and knowledge of neural coding.

claim: Being able to signal fast changes in light inputs might aid the ONα GC retinal circuit in the efficient encoding of dynamic features such as during motion.
source: Second, being able to signal fast changes in light inputs might aid the ONα GC retinal circuit in the efficient encoding of dynamic features such as during motion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and knowledge of neural coding.

claim: Presynaptic inhibition mediated by GABAergic interneurons contributes to motor behavior in the spinal cord, where it controls the gain of sensory afferents and mediates smooth muscle movement.
source: For instance, presynaptic inhibition mediated by GABAergic interneurons contributes to motor behavior in the spinal cord, where it controls the gain of sensory afferents and mediates smooth muscle movement (Fink et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the olfactory system, GABAergic presynaptic inhibition of the olfactory sensory axon terminals serves as a primary gain control mechanism to maintain odor sensitivity over a wide range of inputs.
source: In the olfactory system, GABAergic presynaptic inhibition of the olfactory sensory axon terminals serves as a primary gain control mechanism to maintain odor sensitivity over a wide range of inputs (Olsen and Wilson, 2008; Root et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Presynaptic inhibition mediated by GABA receptors controls temporal contrast enhancement and modifies odor-guided navigation in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Additionally, presynaptic inhibition mediated by GABA receptors controls temporal contrast enhancement and modifies odor-guided navigation in Drosophila melanogaster (Raccuglia et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Excitatory synaptic inputs dictate the spike output of the ONα GCs.
source: Previous studies have shown that excitatory synaptic inputs dictate the spike output of the ONα GCs (Murphy and Rieke, 2006), and we show that GABAA presynaptic inhibition is a key mechanism well-poised to shape the ONα GC excitatory synaptic inputs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: GABAA and GABAC receptors are localized at axon terminals of ON BCs, but they have been shown to be present at spatially distinct sites at RBC terminals relative to the site of synaptic release.
source: Both GABAA and GABAC receptors are localized at axon terminals of ON BCs, but they have been shown to be present at spatially distinct sites at RBC terminals relative to the site of synaptic release, i.e. ribbon (Grimes et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pharmacological blockade and genetic deletion of GABAC receptors have shown that GABAC receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition regulates the extent of multivesicular glutamate release at the bipolar ribbon-type synapses.
source: Pharmacological blockade and genetic deletion of GABAC receptors have shown that GABAC receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition regulates the extent of multivesicular glutamate release at the bipolar ribbon-type synapses (Oesch and Diamond, 2019; Sagdullaev et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of GABAC receptors results in activation of the perisynaptic NMDA receptors on RGC dendrites by glutamate spillover from the synapse thus enhancing synaptic output.
source: Particularly in the ON CBC synapse, loss of GABAC receptors results in activation of the perisynaptic NMDA receptors on RGC dendrites by glutamate spillover from the synapse thus enhancing synaptic output (Sagdullaev et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Glutamate spillover from the synapse could be a potential underlying mechanism for the enhanced light-evoked response observed in ONα GCs in absence of GABAA receptors on the ON CBC terminals.
source: Particularly in the ON CBC synapse, loss of GABAC receptors results in activation of the perisynaptic NMDA receptors on RGC dendrites by glutamate spillover from the synapse thus enhancing synaptic output (Sagdullaev et al., 2006). This could be a potential underlying mechanism for the enhanced light-evoked response we observe in ONα GCs in absence of GABAA receptors on the ON CBC terminals.
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous literature and the current findings.

claim: In RBCs, luminance and contrast are encoded via dynamic release and replenishment of the readily releasable pool of synaptic vesicles located at the ribbon.
source: In RBCs, luminance and contrast are encoded via dynamic release and replenishment of the readily releasable pool (RRP) of synaptic vesicles located at the ribbon (Oesch and Diamond, 2011; Oesch and Diamond, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A step increase in luminance results in contrast encoding via a transient bout of vesicle release from the RRP, which corresponds to a transient peak in the AII AC excitatory current.
source: A step increase in luminance results in contrast encoding via a transient bout of vesicle release from the RRP, which corresponds to a transient peak in the AII AC excitatory current.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about RBC signaling.

claim: The size of the remaining vesicle pool is used to encode luminance and corresponds to the sustained component of the excitatory postsynaptic current.
source: The size of the remaining vesicle pool is used to encode luminance and corresponds to the sustained component of the excitatory postsynaptic current.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about RBC signaling.

claim: A17 AC-mediated feedback inhibition on RBCs acting via GABAC receptors has been implicated in regulating the extent of RRP depletion and synaptic output from RBCs which in turn shapes luminance and contrast encoding across a range of dim light levels.
source: A17 AC-mediated feedback inhibition on RBCs acting via GABAC receptors has been implicated in regulating the extent of RRP depletion and synaptic output from RBCs which in turn shapes luminance and contrast encoding across a range of dim light levels (Oesch and Diamond, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lack of GABAA receptors in the RBC and T6 CBC terminals affects both the transient and sustained components of RBC and T6 CBC output as measured from the impact on the ONα GC excitatory inputs under rod- and cone-dominant light conditions.
source: Our results show that lack of GABAA receptors in the RBC and T6 CBC terminals affects both the transient and sustained components of RBC and T6 CBC output as measured from the impact on the ONα GC excitatory inputs under rod- and cone-dominant light conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings supported by data from Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Both contrast and luminance encoding in the RBC and T6 CBC pathway might be shaped by GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition.
source: This indicates that both contrast and luminance encoding in the RBC and T6 CBC pathway might be shaped by GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing effects on both transient and sustained components.

claim: The input-output relationship of membrane voltage vs. transmitter release is nonlinear and has a sigmoidal shape for most synapses.
source: It is well established that for most synapses the input-output relationship of membrane voltage vs. transmitter release is nonlinear and has a sigmoidal shape (Neher and Sakaba, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The synaptic transfer function of the ON CBC terminals has a sigmoidal relationship between membrane voltage and glutamate release with a steep nonlinear foot.
source: Previous studies have in fact proposed that this synaptic transfer function of the ON CBC terminals has a sigmoidal relationship between membrane voltage and glutamate release with a steep nonlinear foot (Grimes et al., 2014b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The ON CBC presynaptic membrane potential can be influenced by gap junctional coupling from the AII amacrine cell processes which can alter synapse output by changing its location on the voltage-release curve.
source: The ON CBC or presynaptic membrane potential can be influenced by gap junctional coupling from the AII amacrine cell processes which can alter synapse output by changing its location on the voltage-release curve.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about retinal circuitry.

claim: Gap junctional coupling from the AII amacrine cell processes has been shown to play a critical role in shaping ONα GC function.
source: This form of regulating synaptic output has been shown to play a critical role in shaping ONα GC function (Grimes et al., 2014b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition could regulate the presynaptic membrane voltage of the ON CBC, thereby controlling the set point of the synapse input-output curve and hence the ONα GC excitatory inputs.
source: GABAA receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition could also regulate the presynaptic membrane voltage of the ON CBC, thereby controlling the set point of the synapse input-output curve and hence the ONα GC excitatory inputs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on knowledge of presynaptic inhibition mechanisms.

claim: Presynaptic inhibition plays a key role in the precise assembly of the ribbon synapse at the RBC terminal and organization with correct postsynaptic partners.
source: Our recent study showed that presynaptic inhibition plays a key role in the precise assembly of the ribbon synapse at the RBC terminal and organization with correct postsynaptic partners (Sinha et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Under conditions where expression of both GABAA and GABAC receptors in the RBC terminals are downregulated, the RBC ribbon synapse is misorganised and makes erroneous connections with postsynaptic partners.
source: Interestingly, under conditions where expression of both GABAA and GABAC receptors in the RBC terminals are downregulated, such as during lack of global inhibitory transmitter release or loss of specific synaptic adhesion molecules, ultrastructural analysis revealed that the RBC ribbon synapse is misorganised and makes erroneous connections with postsynaptic partners (Sinha et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Despite the downregulation of both GABAA and GABAC receptors at the RBC terminal in situations of global inhibitory transmitter release loss, there is decreased dim light sensitivity of the ONα GC output probably due to a reduced feedforward excitatory drive as a result of synaptic mis-arrangements at the RBC terminal.
source: Therefore, despite the downregulation of both GABAA and GABAC receptors at the RBC terminal in this situation, there is decreased dim light sensitivity of the ONα GC output (Sinha et al., 2020) probably due to a reduced feedforward excitatory drive as a result of synaptic mis-arrangements at the RBC terminal.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and includes an inference about the mechanism.

claim: In the KO mice used in the current study, there is a drastic reduction of GABAA receptor expression but unaltered GABAC receptor expression in the RBC terminals.
source: In the KO mice used in the current study, there is a drastic reduction of GABAA receptor expression but unaltered GABAC receptor expression in the RBC terminals.
evidence: This is supported by data from Figure 1.

claim: The Ai9/Grm6Cre/Gabrg2 triple transgenic mouse line has previously been used to study the subunit composition of GABAA receptors in axon and dendrites of ON CBCs after Gabrg2 deletion.
source: This triple transgenic mouse line – Ai9/Grm6Cre/Gabrg2 cKO (henceforth referred to as KO) – has previously been used to study the subunit composition of GABAA receptors in axon and dendrites of ON CBCs after Gabrg2 deletion (Hoon et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Loss of Gabrg2 causes reduced presence of axonal but not dendritic GABAAα1 receptors in T6 CBCs.
source: Loss of Gabrg2 causes reduced presence of axonal but not dendritic GABAAα1 receptors in T6 CBCs (Hoon et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.
